title: Superlogarithmic clique-versus-independent-set communication
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
formal:
Does there exist a sequence of finite simple undirected graphs \(G_i\), with \(n_i=|V(G_i)|\to\infty\), for which certifying that a clique and an independent set are disjoint requires \(\omega(\log n_i)\) nondeterministic communication? Using the precise separator definition below, the target is
\[\lim_{i\to\infty}\frac{N_0(G_i)}{\log_2 n_i}=\infty.\]
The answer is yes: Göös proved a lower bound \(N_0(G_i)=\Omega((\log n_i)^{1.128})\) for a graph family in 2015. This card records the original source question and its verified published resolution.
why: The question distinguishes the ease of certifying a shared vertex from the difficulty of certifying disjointness under strong graph promises. Its resolution connected communication lower bounds with separator families, unambiguous computation and the polynomial version of the Alon–Saks–Seymour conjecture. It is historically significant but no longer belongs among active open targets.
status_note: Resolved affirmatively by Göös (FOCS 2015), Theorem 1. On 2026-09-14, the source question and original theorem were checked directly, including their opposite intersection/disjointness output conventions. The proved lower bound already exceeds logarithmic communication; the later 2026 optimal-bound claim is unnecessary to this conclusion.

sentences: Alice receives a clique and Bob an independent set in the same public graph.
Certifying that their sets intersect is easy because a shared vertex is a short certificate.
The historical question asks whether certifying disjointness can require more than any constant multiple of the logarithm of the graph size.
Göös answered yes in 2015 with a lower bound of order the logarithm raised to the power 1.128.
The card is archived as resolved, with newer claimed improvements recorded separately.

definitions:
For a graph \(G=(V,E)\) on \(n\ge2\) labelled vertices, a clique \(C\subseteq V\) has every pair of distinct vertices adjacent, while an independent set \(I\subseteq V\) has no adjacent pair. Alice receives \(C\), Bob receives \(I\), and both know the entire graph without paying communication to describe it. Their sets intersect in at most one vertex. The output being certified is disjointness, \(C\cap I=\varnothing\); certifying a nonempty intersection is a different, easier task.

A separating family is a finite collection \(\mathcal S\subseteq2^V\) such that, for every disjoint clique–independent-set pair \((C,I)\), there is \(S\in\mathcal S\) with \(C\subseteq S\) and \(S\cap I=\varnothing\). Let \(q(G)\) be the minimum size of such a family, and define \(N_0(G)=\lceil\log_2 q(G)\rceil\). A separating family always exists, for example by taking all subsets of \(V\), so this finite minimum is well-defined. Empty cliques and independent sets are permitted.

This is the certificate convention for nondeterministic communication: an untrusted prover supplies both parties an index of a separator; Alice checks containment and Bob checks avoidance locally. A disjoint pair must have an index that both accept, and an intersecting pair must have none. More generally a certificate labels a rectangle \(\mathcal C\times\mathcal I\) consisting entirely of disjoint pairs. Such a rectangle is contained in the separator rectangle for \(S=\bigcup_{C\in\mathcal C} C\), so allowing arbitrary locally checkable certificates gives the same minimum cover. Counting final acceptance bits changes cost by at most a constant and has no effect on the target. Local computation, the public graph and protocol descriptions are unrestricted; no randomized error is allowed.

The limit statement means that for every real \(M>0\) there is \(i_0\) such that \(N_0(G_i)\ge M\log_2 n_i\) for every \(i\ge i_0\). An unbounded subsequence of graph sizes suffices; a graph on every integer size is not required. Equivalently, the required number of separators grows faster than every fixed polynomial in \(n_i\).
answer_criterion: For the original benchmark question, supply a graph-family construction and a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the superlogarithmic lower bound. A lower bound only for deterministic protocols would not establish the stated nondeterministic target. A fixed constant multiple of \(\log n\) also does not suffice. The 2015 mathematical resolution establishes the positive answer; this editorial review does not claim to supply its Lean formalization.

context_blocks.text: Naming the shared vertex certifies intersection using \(\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\) bits. The source asks about certificates for the opposite answer, for which a deterministic \(O((\log n)^2)\) protocol was known.

The source defines its Boolean function to be one on disjoint pairs. Göös defines CIS to be one on intersecting pairs and consequently calls the same disjointness lower bound conondeterministic. The difference is only output convention; the theorem matches this card’s target.

Göös’s Theorem 1 gives an exponent strictly larger than one and explicitly identifies Jukna’s Research Problem 4.15 as an open question it resolves. Since \((\log n)^{1.128}/\log n\to\infty\), this is sufficient without determining the optimal exponent.

The August 2026 preprint claims a further improvement to the optimal quadratic-logarithmic scale. That newer claim is not needed for the archival decision, which rests on the published 2015 resolution.
